lessons.title: Matrices: types, operations, product and transpose
lessons.slides: Lecturer's notes p.1; past test Q5, Q10, Q12
lessons.one_line: A matrix is a grid of numbers that you can add, scale, multiply and flip, and the order in which you multiply matters.
lessons.analogy: A matrix is a spreadsheet: rows run across, columns run down. Multiplying two spreadsheets means pairing each row of the first with each column of the second and adding up the products, the way you total a price list against a quantity list.
recall: A grid has 3 rows and 2 columns. How many numbers does it hold?
Is 3 times 4 the same as 4 times 3? Do you think the same is true when you multiply two grids of numbers?
exam: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers (called entries) arranged in rows and columns. A matrix with $m$ rows and $n$ columns has order $m\times n$. The entry $a_{ij}$ is in row $i$, column $j$.
Special matrices: a square matrix has $m=n$; a row matrix has one row; a column matrix has one column; a zero matrix has every entry $0$.
The identity matrix $I$ is square with $1$ on the main diagonal and $0$ everywhere else, so $AI=IA=A$.

Two matrices are equal only if they have the same order and equal corresponding entries. Addition and subtraction work entry by entry and need the same order. The scalar multiple $kA$ multiplies every entry by $k$.

The product $AB$ exists only if the number of columns of $A$ equals the number of rows of $B$. If $A$ is $m\times n$ and $B$ is $n\times p$, then $AB$ is $m\times p$, and $(AB)_{ij}=\sum_k a_{ik}b_{kj}$: row $i$ of $A$ times column $j$ of $B$.
Matrix multiplication is generally not commutative: $AB\neq BA$, even when both products exist. It is associative, $(AB)C=A(BC)$, and distributive, $A(B+C)=AB+AC$.

The transpose $A^{T}$ is formed by interchanging rows and columns: the first row becomes the first column, and so on. If $A$ is $m\times n$, then $A^{T}$ is $n\times m$. Rules: $(A^{T})^{T}=A$, $(A+B)^{T}=A^{T}+B^{T}$, $(AB)^{T}=B^{T}A^{T}$.
A matrix with non-negative entries whose rows each sum to $1$ is called a stochastic matrix. It appears in the past test (Q12); the name is standard but is not in your notes.

examples.title: Product and transpose (from your notes)

steps.why: A is 2 by 3 and B is 3 by 2. The columns of A (3) equal the rows of B (3), so AB exists, and it is 2 by 2.

steps.do: Top-left entry: row 1 of A times column 1 of B.
Top-right entry: row 1 of A times column 2 of B.
Bottom-left entry: row 2 of A times column 1 of B.
Bottom-right entry: row 2 of A times column 2 of B.

steps.why: The first row (35, 79) becomes the first column; the second row (20, 32) becomes the second column.

examples.answer: $AB=\begin{bmatrix}35&79\\20&32\end{bmatrix}$ and $(AB)^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}35&20\\79&32\end{bmatrix}$. Check: $B^{T}A^{T}$ gives the same matrix.

examples.title: AB is not BA (past test question 10)
examples.problem: If $A=\begin{bmatrix}6&0&4\\1&5&-3\end{bmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{bmatrix}2&9\\8&0\\-4&7\end{bmatrix}$, find $A\cdot B$ and $B\cdot A$.

steps.why: A is 2 by 3 and B is 3 by 2. AB is 2 by 2 and BA is 3 by 3, so both exist, but they have different orders and cannot be equal.

steps.do: Row 1 of A against the two columns of B.
Row 2 of A against the two columns of B.
Now BA. Row 1 of B is (2, 9), and the columns of A are (6, 1), (0, 5), (4, -3).

examples.answer: $AB=\begin{bmatrix}-4&82\\54&-12\end{bmatrix}$ and $BA=\begin{bmatrix}21&45&-19\\48&0&32\\-17&35&-37\end{bmatrix}$. They are not even the same size.

practice.hint: Row 1 of A times column 1 of B is 1(0)+2(1).
solution: Multiply row by column for each entry.

practice.hint: The first row becomes the first column.
solution: Rows become columns: the 3 by 2 matrix becomes 2 by 3.

practice.q: What is the order of the product of a 3 by 2 matrix and a 2 by 4 matrix? Answer like 5x6.
practice.hint: Columns of the first (2) must equal rows of the second (2). The result keeps the outer numbers.
solution: Inner numbers match (2 and 2), so the product exists.
The result keeps the outer numbers: 3 by 4.

practice.q: With $A=\begin{bmatrix}6&0&4\\1&5&-3\end{bmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{bmatrix}2&9\\8&0\\-4&7\end{bmatrix}$, what is the entry in row 2, column 1 of $AB$?
practice.hint: Row 2 of A is (1, 5, -3). Column 1 of B is (2, 8, -4).

solution.do: Row 2 of A times column 1 of B.

practice.hint: BA is 3 by 3. Each row of B is paired with each column of A.

solution.do: Work through the three rows of B.

practice.q: Using $A$ and $B$ from the lecturer's example, $A=\begin{bmatrix}2&7&6\\3&1&5\end{bmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{bmatrix}4&0\\3&7\\1&5\end{bmatrix}$, find $(AB)^{T}$.
practice.hint: Find AB first, then swap rows and columns.

practice.q: A stochastic matrix has rows that each sum to 1. For what value of $x$ is $\begin{bmatrix}0.7&x\\0.4&0.6\end{bmatrix}$ stochastic?

solution.do: Set the first row sum to 1.

solution: The second row already sums to 0.4 + 0.6 = 1.

quiz.q: For which pair does the product AB exist?
quiz.explain: The columns of A (3) must equal the rows of B (3). The result is 2x4.

quiz.q: If A is 3x5, what is the order of A transpose?
quiz.explain: Rows and columns swap, so the order flips to 5x3.

quiz.q: Which statement about the identity matrix I is correct?
options: AI = A only when A is zero
quiz.explain: I has 1s on the main diagonal and 0s elsewhere, and multiplying by it leaves a matrix unchanged.

quiz.q: The product BA exists and AB exists, and both are square but of different sizes. What does this show?
options: A and B are identity matrices
quiz.explain: Matrices of different orders cannot be equal, so AB is not BA. In general matrix multiplication is not commutative.

flashcards.back: When the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B. An m by n times n by p gives m by p.

flashcards.front: What does the identity matrix look like?
flashcards.back: Square, 1s on the main diagonal, 0s elsewhere. AI = IA = A.
Not in general. Matrix multiplication is not commutative.
Non-negative entries, and each row sums to 1.

matrix.plain: A grid of numbers in rows and columns.
matrix.exam: A rectangular array of numbers (entries) arranged in rows and columns.

order.plain: How many rows by how many columns.
order.exam: A matrix with m rows and n columns has order m by n.

entry.exam: The element a_ij in row i and column j.

square-matrix.plain: A grid with as many rows as columns.

identity-matrix.plain: The matrix version of the number 1.
identity-matrix.exam: Square matrix with 1s on the main diagonal and 0s elsewhere; AI = IA = A.

zero-matrix.exam: A matrix in which every entry is 0.

transpose.plain: Flip the grid so rows become columns.
transpose.exam: A transpose is obtained by interchanging rows and columns; an m by n matrix becomes n by m.

scalar.plain: An ordinary number, not a grid.
scalar.exam: A single number used to multiply every entry of a matrix.

stochastic-matrix.plain: A grid of probabilities where each row adds up to 1.
stochastic-matrix.exam: A matrix with non-negative entries whose rows each sum to 1 (name is standard, not in the notes).

row-column.plain: Rows go across; columns go down.
row-column.exam: Horizontal and vertical lines of entries in a matrix.

commutative.exam: An operation is commutative if the order of the operands does not change the result. Matrix multiplication is not.
